scenes.narration: Ten in the morning. A giant box with no windows, concrete floors and steel racks up to the ceiling. The doors open, and half the crowd walks right past the televisions, to the back corner, for a hot dog and a soda. Price? a dollar fifty. Reportedly, the same price since nineteen eighty-five.

And yet this is one of the most profitable retailers in America. In its last fiscal year, Costco sold two hundred and ninety-seven billion dollars worth of goods and earned nine point two billion dollars. But on the goods themselves, it makes almost nothing. So where do the billions come from?
Let's follow the money. The thinnest margin in the building, a plastic card, a very short shopping list, a very cheap hot dog, and the money Costco holds before it pays anyone.

Start with the size. Costco began operations in Seattle in nineteen eighty-three. By the end of fiscal twenty twenty-six, it ran nine hundred and thirty-nine warehouses, and today it has nine hundred and forty-five, from Iceland to New Zealand. Net sales grew about ten percent in a single year.

Now look at what it keeps. Gross margin, what's left after paying for the goods, was eleven point one percent of sales. By our calculation, the average item sells for only about twelve and a half percent more than it cost. Costco's own annual report says it operates at significantly lower gross margins than most other retailers.

Let me draw one hundred dollars at the register. About eighty-nine dollars goes straight back to the suppliers. That leaves about eleven. Around nine of those pay for the warehouses, the workers and the trucks. What's left from selling the goods, by our calculation, is about two dollars. Two dollars, out of a hundred.

keyframes.cue: Two dollars, out of a hundred
keyframes.label: strokes[5].start.cue

scenes.narration: Then there's the other line on the income statement. Membership fees. five point nine billion dollars in a single year. That's equal to about half of Costco's operating income, the profit from running the business before interest and taxes, which was eleven point seven billion dollars. Fees have their own costs, so they aren't pure profit. But they arrive before you've bought a single thing.
So the store floor is almost a break-even machine. The real business sits at a little desk by the front door.

To shop here, you need a card. At the end of fiscal twenty twenty-six, Costco had eighty-four million paid members, and about one hundred and fifty million cardholders once the extra household cards are counted. In the United States, the basic card costs sixty-five dollars a year, and it comes with a free second card for someone in your household.

And they come back. The renewal rate was ninety-two point three percent in the United States and Canada, and eighty-nine point eight percent worldwide. That's a fee you pay every year, before you buy anything. And more than nine out of ten people pay it again.

keyframes.cue: more than nine out of ten
keyframes.label: cam[2].at.cue

keyframes.cue: more than nine out of ten
keyframes.label: items[11].at.cue

keyframes.cue: more than nine out of ten
keyframes.label: items[12].faces[1][0].cue

scenes.narration: Let me chart the price of that card in the United States. Fifty dollars, until late twenty eleven. Then fifty-five. In twenty seventeen, sixty. And in September twenty twenty-four, sixty-five. A small step, every six or seven years. And each time, renewal rates stayed around nine in ten.

That last increase touched around fifty-two million memberships. The Executive card went from one hundred and twenty to one hundred and thirty dollars. And Costco says the higher fee explained only about thirty percent of the growth in membership income in fiscal twenty twenty-six. The rest came from new members and upgrades.

And here's a quiet detail. Costco doesn't count your fee as income on the day you pay it. It spreads it over the twelve months of your membership. So at the end of fiscal twenty twenty-six, members had already handed over about three billion dollars that Costco hadn't even counted yet. Next year's income, sitting in the bank.

Those upgrades matter. Executive members pay double, and earn about two percent back on what they buy, up to a yearly cap. There are about forty-two million of them. By our calculation, that's about half of all paid members. And they account for about seventy-five percent of Costco's sales.

See the trick? The fee makes you come back to get your money's worth. The reward makes you spend more when you do. In fiscal twenty seventeen, membership fees were two point nine billion dollars. Last fiscal year, five point nine billion dollars. More than double.

Next, the shelves. Costco says it carries fewer than four thousand active items per warehouse, significantly fewer than other big retailers. Not twenty kinds of ketchup. One or two, in giant packs, still sitting on the pallet.

A short list means every item sells in enormous volume. Enormous volume means bargaining power with the companies that make the goods. And the goods arrive on pallets, stored on racks above the floor, which Costco says reduces the labor needed.

The list also keeps moving. Costco says it adjusts the items it sells to focus on the most productive ones. Shoppers call it the treasure hunt. If you see it, you'd better buy it, because next week it might be gone.

And then there's the house brand. In his latest letter to shareholders, chief executive Ron Vachris wrote that Kirkland Signature now brings in about ninety billion dollars a year worldwide, typically saving members fifteen to twenty percent compared with the national brand.

By our rough calculation, that's about a third of Costco's sales. And according to its annual report, these products generally earn Costco higher margins. The cheaper box for you is the better deal for Costco. And Costco says it expects to keep increasing the share of its sales that comes from its own label.

Let me draw the squeeze. Here's a typical supermarket. A long list, each item selling a little. Here's Costco. A short list, each item selling a lot. Big volume per item means a strong hand with the supplier. The house brand is a second lever. Both push the price down.

keyframes.cue: a strong hand with the supplier
keyframes.label: strokes[4].start.cue

scenes.narration: Now, the food court. When speculation spread in twenty twenty-four that the hot dog combo might finally go up, Costco's finance chief told analysts, quote, the dollar-fifty hot dog price is safe.

Co-founder Jim Sinegal, who was chief executive until the start of twenty twelve, put it simply in a newspaper interview, as quoted by CNN. We're known for that hot dog. That's something you don't mess with.

keyframes.cue: We're known for that hot dog
keyframes.label: cam[1].at.cue

scenes.narration: Why protect it? Because the food court isn't really a restaurant. Costco's annual report groups it with gas, pharmacy and optical, as side businesses that, it says, encourage more frequent shopping. A cheap lunch is a reason to come in. The pharmacy, the optical counter and the tire shop do the same job. And every visit passes the pallets.

Gas works the same way, at a bigger scale. Costco ran seven hundred and seventy-four gas stations at the end of fiscal twenty twenty-six, and gasoline was eleven percent of its net sales. Fill up the tank, and while you're here...
Then there's the cash. In Costco's own words, it often sells inventory before it is required to pay for it, even while taking advantage of early payment discounts.

At the end of fiscal twenty twenty-six, it held nineteen point three billion dollars of merchandise. And it owed its suppliers twenty-two point six billion dollars. It owed more than everything on its shelves was worth. That's the quiet superpower of a store where nothing sits still.

Let me draw the clock. Day zero, a pallet arrives. By our calculation, Costco's inventory turns over about fourteen times a year, so a typical item is gone in less than a month. The member pays at the register. Only later does the supplier's bill come due. In between, that money works for Costco.

keyframes.cue: gone in less than a month
keyframes.label: strokes[4].start.cue

scenes.narration: So who pays for all those low prices? Not the workers, Costco argues. Its letter put the average U.S. hourly wage at about thirty-two dollars in twenty twenty-five, and its annual report calls pay its largest expense after the goods themselves. It employed about three hundred and fifty-five thousand people worldwide at the end of fiscal twenty twenty-six.

And the shareholders? On November tenth, twenty twenty-six, Costco declared a special dividend of thirty dollars a share. About thirteen point three billion dollars in total. By our calculation, that's more than two years of membership fees, paid out in one go.

But the whole machine rests on one promise. Costco's own annual report says membership loyalty and growth are essential to its business, and that damage to its reputation could reduce renewal rates. If the savings ever stop beating the fee, the card stops making sense.

Let me put the machine together. Low prices bring members in. Members pay fees, equal to about half the operating profit. A short list sells in huge volume, which keeps prices low. Fast sales let Costco hold its suppliers' money. And the hot dog keeps you coming back. Every part feeds the next.

So how does Costco make billions selling almost nothing? It barely profits on the goods at all. It sells access. The low prices are the product, and the card is the business. The store is the bait. The fee is the catch. And the dollar-fifty hot dog? That's the reminder, every single visit, that the deal is still on.
